title: Software Practice: Version Control, Testing and Reproducibility
description: Git, automated tests for numerical and machine learning code, debugging, reproducible environments and experiments, and code quality.
overview: Machine learning code fails in an unusual way: it often runs without error and returns a wrong answer. A sign flipped in a gradient, a shuffled label column, test data leaking into training, or a broadcast that silently produced the wrong shape all give a model that trains and reports reasonable numbers. The defenses are the same as in other software, applied with extra care: keep a history of changes, test the pieces, make runs reproducible, and write code that can be read.

This chapter covers version control with Git, automated tests (including the tests that are specific to numerical and learning code), debugging, reproducible environments and experiments, and the habits that keep a research project maintainable.
objectives: Use Git for commits, branches and merges, and explain what should and should not be under version control.
Write unit tests with assertions and tolerances, and apply the machine-learning-specific tests: shape checks, gradient checks and overfitting a tiny batch.
Debug systematically with minimal examples, tracebacks, a debugger and bisection.
Make experiments reproducible with pinned environments, seeds, configuration files and logged runs.
Organize a project and write readable, documented code.

sections.title: Version control with Git
body: Anyone who has saved files as report_final.doc, report_final2.doc and report_FINAL_really.doc has felt the problem version control solves. It keeps one clean history of a project, so every earlier state can be recovered, and several people (or several experiments) can work on separate copies and merge the results later without confusion. **Version control** records the history of a project as a series of snapshots, called **commits**, each with a message, an author and a pointer to its parent. It lets you undo mistakes, compare versions, try ideas on **branches** without breaking working code, and collaborate. **Git** is the standard tool. A **repository** is the project folder plus its history.

code: git init                          # start a repository in this folder
git add train.py utils.py         # choose files for the next snapshot
git commit -m 'Add mini-batch loader'    # record the snapshot
git log --oneline                 # history, one line per commit
git switch -c try-adam            # create and switch to a new branch
git merge try-adam                # bring the branch's commits into main
body.caption: The everyday Git commands.

list: Make **small, focused commits** with messages that say why: 'Fix off-by-one in batch loader', not 'changes'. Small commits are easy to review, revert and bisect.
A **merge conflict** arises when two branches change the same lines. Git marks the conflict in the file; you edit it into the desired result and commit.
On a hosting site (GitHub, GitLab), a **pull request** proposes merging a branch and invites review.

List files that should not be tracked in **.gitignore**: virtual environments, caches (__pycache__), notebooks' outputs, and above all large data files, model checkpoints and **secrets** (API keys, passwords). Anything committed stays in history even if later deleted.
Git is poor at large binary files. Track data and models with a tool built for them (Git LFS, DVC) or store them separately and record their version and hash.
`git bisect` finds the commit that introduced a bug by binary search over history, in about log₂(n) steps: for 1000 commits, 10 tests.

check.q: A file with an API key was committed and later deleted. The key
check.a: is still in the repository history and should be considered exposed
wrong: is gone, since the file was deleted
cannot be found by anyone
is encrypted by Git

sections.title: Automated testing
body: A test is a question to which you already know the answer. If your function should add 2 and 3 to give 5, run it and check that it does. Doing this for a handful of cases, automatically, means that when you change the code next month you find out in seconds whether you broke something, rather than weeks later when a result looks strange. A **unit test** is a small program that calls one piece of code with known inputs and checks the output with **assertions**. Tests document how the code should behave, catch mistakes the moment they are introduced, and let you change the code later without fear. The **pytest** framework finds functions named test_* and reports which fail.

code: z = np.array([[1., 2., 3.], [1000., 1001., 1002.]])   # the second row would overflow naively
body.caption: Tests with a known value and with mathematical properties. Run them with `pytest`.

list: **Compare floating-point numbers with a tolerance** (np.testing.assert_allclose, math.isclose), never with ==. See Numerical Computing for why.

**Test properties, not only examples**: probabilities are non-negative and sum to one; a loss is non-negative; shifting inputs does not change softmax; a rotation preserves norms; the prediction of a model must not change if the batch order changes.
**Test edge cases**: empty input, one example, all-equal values, very large and very small numbers, NaN.
**Regression tests**: when you fix a bug, add a test that fails without the fix, so it cannot come back.
**Continuous integration** runs the tests automatically on every push, so that a broken change is caught immediately.
Seed all randomness in tests, or the tests become flaky.

body.h: Tests specific to machine learning code

code: """Central-difference gradient of a scalar function f at array x."""
loss = lambda t: 0.5 * np.mean((X @ t - y) ** 2)
body.caption: A gradient check: compare the hand-derived gradient with a finite difference (see Backpropagation).

list: **Shape tests**: assert the shapes of intermediate arrays, since broadcasting can hide errors. Put assert X.shape == (m, n) in the code itself.
**Overfit a tiny batch**: a model should drive the loss to nearly zero on a handful of examples. If it cannot, the code has a bug.
**Initial loss**: for K balanced classes with random weights the cross-entropy should be about ln K.
**Invariance tests**: permuting the training examples should not change a full-batch result; scaling the learning rate to zero should leave the model unchanged.
**Leakage tests**: assert that the indices of the training, validation and test sets are disjoint.

check.q: How should two floating-point results be compared in a test?
check.a: With a tolerance, as in np.testing.assert_allclose
wrong: With ==
By printing both and looking
By converting them to strings

check.q: What does a gradient check compare?
check.a: The analytic gradient with a finite-difference estimate
wrong: The training loss with the test loss
Two different optimizers
The gradient on two different batches

sections.title: Debugging
body: Debugging is the scientific method applied to code: form a hypothesis about what is wrong, test it, and narrow down. A systematic approach beats guessing.

list: **Read the traceback** from the bottom: the last line says what went wrong, and the lines above give the chain of calls that led to it. The failing line in your own code is usually the one to look at.

**Reproduce it reliably**: fix the random seed and the input. Then make it small: a **minimal reproducible example** with the smallest data and fewest lines that still show the problem. Half of bugs are found while making one.

**Look at the values**: print shapes, dtypes and a few values at each step, or use a debugger. In Python, `breakpoint()` opens the pdb debugger at that line, where you can inspect variables, step line by line and continue.

**Bisect**: find where the computation first goes wrong by checking the intermediate result halfway through the pipeline, then halfway into the bad half. `git bisect` does the same over the history of commits.
**Change one thing at a time**, and keep the previous working version.
**Explain the code aloud** (rubber duck debugging): stating what each line should do reveals the line that does not.

head: Symptom
Likely causes
rows: Learning rate too high; log(0) or division by zero; overflow in exp (use stable softmax); bad data containing NaN
Gradient step with the wrong sign; learning rate far too small; labels not aligned with inputs; no gradient flowing (a detached tensor, a ReLU that is always off)
Training accuracy is great, validation is at chance
Leakage between sets would make validation too good, so look for a train/eval mode mismatch or differently preprocessed validation data
Test or validation data in the training set; normalization statistics computed on all the data; duplicates across splits
Unseeded randomness; non-deterministic GPU operations; data order
Shape errors or silent wrong shapes
Broadcasting a (m,) vector against (m, 1); forgetting keepdims; mixing row and column vectors
table.caption: Frequent failure signatures.

example.title: A NaN hunt
example.problem: The loss becomes NaN after step 137. How do you find the cause?
example.solution: Reproduce with the same seed. Check the inputs of step 137 for NaN or infinity (np.isnan(batch).any()). Print the loss and the gradient norm over the previous steps: a sudden rise indicates divergence, so lower the learning rate or clip gradients. If the gradient is fine, check the operations that can overflow or produce log(0): the softmax, the cross-entropy and any division. Add np.errstate(all='raise') or enable the framework's anomaly detection to stop at the first invalid operation.

wrong: on the first line
in the middle
it is never shown

sections.title: Reproducible environments and experiments
body: A result that cannot be reproduced cannot be trusted, by others or by you in six months. Reproducibility has four ingredients.

list: **Code**: the exact version, a Git commit hash, recorded with each run.

**Environment**: the Python version and the versions of all libraries. Use a **virtual environment** and a **requirements file** with pinned versions (numpy==1.26.4), or a lock file, or a container (Docker) for the whole system, GPU libraries included.

**Data**: the exact data and the split. Keep raw data read-only and generate processed versions with scripts; record hashes or versions. Fix the train/validation/test split once, by seed or by an explicit list of ids.

**Randomness**: seeds for every source (Python's random, NumPy, the deep learning framework), noting that some GPU operations are non-deterministic and some libraries change their generators between versions.

body: Do not scatter magic numbers through the code. Put hyperparameters in a configuration file or a dataclass (see Python for Machine Learning), pass it to the training function, and save it next to the results. For every run, log the configuration, the code version, the seed, the metrics over time and the final result, either in a simple CSV/JSON file or with a tracking tool (MLflow, Weights & Biases, TensorBoard). Save **checkpoints** of the model so that long runs can resume, and the best model can be recovered.

body.caption: A minimal experiment log: one JSON line per run with the configuration, the Git commit and the metrics.

body: Jupyter notebooks mix code, results and text, which makes them excellent for exploration and communication. They hide state (cells can be run out of order) and diff badly in version control. A good pattern: explore in a notebook, then move the reusable code into modules that are tested and imported by notebooks and scripts. Restart the kernel and run all cells before trusting or sharing a notebook.

body.warn: Report the variation, not one run. A model trained with ten seeds shows the spread caused by initialization and data order; differences smaller than that spread are noise (see Evaluating Models).

check.q: Which items should be recorded with every experiment run?
check.a: The configuration, the code version and the random seed
wrong: Only the final accuracy
Only the model weights
The name of the person who ran it

sections.title: Code quality and project structure
body: Code is read far more often than it is written, including by its author a month later. A few habits make research code survive.

list: **Name things for what they mean**: learning_rate, not lr2; X_train, not data1. A function name should say what it returns or does.
**Small functions that do one thing**, with explicit inputs and outputs. Avoid hidden global state. A function that takes a configuration and a random generator is easy to test and reuse.
**Do not repeat yourself**: copy-pasted code is copied bugs. Extract the common part into a function.

**Document the why**: docstrings state the purpose, the shapes and the units; comments explain choices that are not obvious ('subtract max for numerical stability'). Do not comment what the code plainly says.

**Use tools**: a formatter (black, ruff format) ends arguments about layout, a linter (ruff, flake8) catches unused variables and likely bugs, and a type checker (mypy) catches wrong argument types. Run them automatically.
**Review**: a second reader finds the bugs and unclear parts that the author cannot see. In research code, review at least the data pipeline and the evaluation.

code: README.md            what it is, how to run it, how to reproduce the results
src/mylib/           importable code: data.py, models.py, train.py, evaluate.py
data/                raw (read-only) and processed data, not in Git
body.caption: A layout that separates code, configuration, data and results.

body.tip: Refactor in small steps with the tests passing at every step. Change the structure of the code without changing its behavior, and run the tests after each change; if they stay green, the behavior is preserved. Without tests, refactoring is guessing.

check.q: Why keep raw data read-only and generate processed data with scripts?
check.a: The processing can be repeated and audited, and the original is never altered by accident
wrong: It makes files smaller
It makes the model more accurate
It is required by Git

quiz.q: Two branches each edit the same line of train.py differently, and one is merged into the other. What happens?
quiz.a: A merge conflict is reported; you edit the marked lines and commit
wrong: Git keeps the version from the branch with the newer commit and discards the other
Git keeps both versions as two separate files
Git refuses ever to merge the branches
quiz.why: Git can combine changes to different lines automatically, but when both sides change the same lines it cannot know which to keep, so a person must resolve it.

quiz.q: A bug appeared somewhere in a history of 4096 commits, with the first commit known to be good. About how many tests does git bisect need to find the culprit?
quiz.why: Each test halves the range of suspect commits, so about log₂(4096) = 12 tests are enough. Testing the commits one by one would take thousands.

quiz.q: A 5 GB image data set is part of a project that is kept in Git. What is the recommended practice?
quiz.a: Use DVC or Git LFS, or store it elsewhere and record its version and hash
wrong: Commit it normally, because Git compresses binary files efficiently enough
Commit it once and then add it to .gitignore so that later commits skip it
Commit the data in 100 MB pieces so that each single commit stays small
quiz.why: Git is poor at large binary files, and anything committed stays in history even if deleted later. Recording a version or hash keeps the data traceable without bloating the repository.

quiz.q: Why does a test of softmax include an input row such as [1000, 1001, 1002]?
quiz.a: A naive exp overflows here, so it is an edge case
wrong: It checks that the outputs add up to something larger than 1 when inputs are large
It confirms that softmax changes when a constant is added to every input
It makes the test run faster, since large numbers need fewer steps
quiz.why: exp(1000) overflows, so only an implementation that subtracts the maximum passes. Softmax is shift invariant, and its outputs always sum to 1.

quiz.q: A central-difference gradient check with eps = 0.1 is applied to f(x) = x² at x = 3. What estimate does it give?
quiz.why: (f(3.1) - f(2.9)) / 0.2 = (9.61 - 8.41)/0.2 = 6.0, equal to the true derivative 2x. The forward difference would give 6.1 and the backward difference 5.9.

quiz.q: A balanced 100-class classifier with random weights shows an initial cross-entropy loss of about 4.6. What does this indicate?
quiz.a: Nothing; ln 100 ≈ 4.6 is the loss of a uniform prediction
wrong: The learning rate is too high, because losses should start near 1 at the beginning
The labels are misaligned, because a correct model would start near 0
The model is already overfitting the training set from the first step
quiz.why: A uniform prediction over K classes gives a loss of ln K. A value far from that, such as 40, would point to a bug or a bad weight scale.

quiz.q: A network cannot reach a near-zero training loss on a batch of just 8 examples. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
quiz.a: There is probably a bug in the code
wrong: The network needs far more training examples before the loss can fall
The data set is too small to measure anything meaningful about the model
This is normal, because a model cannot memorize as few as 8 examples
quiz.why: A model of reasonable size can memorize a handful of examples. If it cannot, the fault is likely in the code (the gradient, the labels or the update) rather than the amount of data.

quiz.q: You fix a bug where the batch loader dropped the last partial batch. Which new test is the best regression test?
quiz.a: One that fails on the old buggy code and passes on the fixed code
wrong: One that passes both before and after the fix
One that only checks that the loader runs without raising an exception
One that compares the loader's speed before and after the fix
quiz.why: A regression test earns its keep by detecting the bug if it ever returns. A test that also passes on the buggy code proves nothing about the fix.

quiz.q: Training loss was fine until step 137, then NaN. The gradient norm rose steeply over the previous steps. Which cause fits best?
quiz.a: Divergence from too high a learning rate
wrong: Labels that are not aligned with the inputs after shuffling
Unseeded randomness in the data loader order
Validation data that leaked into the training set
quiz.why: A steadily growing gradient norm followed by NaN is the signature of divergence, treated by lowering the learning rate or clipping gradients. Misaligned labels would give a loss that never falls, not a blow-up.

quiz.q: A training loss stays flat from the first step, and a code review finds the update theta += lr * grad. What is the problem?
quiz.a: The step has the wrong sign
wrong: The learning rate is too high and causes oscillation around the minimum
The gradient is computed on the validation set rather than the training set
The random seed is not fixed, so every run starts differently
quiz.why: Gradient descent subtracts the gradient. Adding it moves uphill, so the loss does not decrease (or grows).

quiz.q: Validation accuracy is suspiciously close to perfect. The code standardizes features using the mean and standard deviation of the whole data set before splitting. What is wrong?
quiz.a: Validation information leaks into the preprocessing, so the score is optimistic
wrong: The standard deviation should have been computed with n - 1 degrees of freedom
The validation set is too small to be standardized in a meaningful way
Standardizing before the split changes the training labels as well as the features
quiz.why: The statistics were computed using validation rows, so the evaluation is no longer on unseen data. The statistics should come from the training split only and then be applied to the others.

quiz.q: An 8-stage data pipeline gives a wrong final output, and the output after stage 4 is correct. Which check best continues a bisection?
wrong: Inspect the output after stage 2
Inspect the output after stage 8 again
Rewrite stages 1 to 4 first
quiz.why: The fault must lie in stages 5 to 8. Checking the middle of that range, after stage 6, halves the remaining possibilities again.

quiz.q: Two people run the same commit with the same seed and get different accuracies. One of them is on a new machine. Which ingredient of reproducibility was most likely not recorded?
wrong: The Git commit hash of the code that was run
The random seed used for initialization
The name of the person who ran the script
quiz.why: The code and seed were identical, so the remaining candidate is a different environment, for example a library whose algorithms or generator changed between versions. Pinned versions or a container prevent this.

quiz.q: Over 10 seeds, model A has a mean accuracy of 91.2% and model B 91.4%, and the standard deviation across seeds is about 0.5% for both. What is the fair conclusion?
quiz.a: The gap is within seed-to-seed noise, so B is not shown to be better
wrong: B is better, because its mean accuracy is higher than that of A
A is better, because 91.2% is closer to a round number
Neither model works, since the standard deviation is nonzero
quiz.why: A difference much smaller than the spread produced by initialization and data order is not evidence of a real improvement. More seeds or a larger gap would be needed.

quiz.q: A notebook's final cell gives a good result that depends on a variable defined in a cell that was later deleted. Which habit would have exposed the problem?
quiz.a: Restarting the kernel and running all cells
wrong: Printing the variable once before sharing the notebook
Committing the notebook with all outputs saved
Running only the last cell again
quiz.why: Notebooks keep hidden state in memory, and cells can run out of order. A clean restart runs the notebook the way a new reader would.

quiz.q: A 3,000-line module is being refactored to separate data loading from training. Which approach is recommended?
quiz.a: Make small structural changes and run the tests after each one
wrong: Rewrite the whole module first and then write tests for the new version
Change the structure and the model's behavior in the same step to save time
Skip the tests, because refactoring does not change behavior
quiz.why: Tests that stay green after each small step show that behavior is preserved. Without tests, restructuring is guessing.

quiz.q: The same preprocessing code is copied into both train.py and evaluate.py. What is the main danger of this copy-paste?
quiz.a: A bug fixed in one copy stays in the other, so training and evaluation can quietly diverge
wrong: Python refuses to import two files that contain identical blocks of code
The tests can no longer assert the shapes of intermediate arrays
It makes the repository too large for Git to store efficiently
quiz.why: Copied code means copied bugs, and later fixes reach only one copy. Extracting a shared function keeps both stages consistent.

summary: Git records snapshots (commits), supports branches and merges, and needs a .gitignore that excludes data, environments and secrets. Small commits with clear messages, and git bisect, make history useful.

Unit tests assert known values and mathematical properties, with tolerances for floats. Learning code needs extra tests: shapes, gradient checks, the initial loss, overfitting a tiny batch and leakage checks.

Debug systematically: read the traceback, make a minimal reproducible example, inspect values, bisect and change one thing at a time. Learn the signatures of common failures (NaN, flat loss, too-good validation).
Reproducibility needs the code version, pinned environment, fixed data splits and seeds, a configuration file and a run log. Report spread across seeds.
Write readable code with clear names, small functions and tools (formatter, linter, tests, review), and keep a clean project structure.

problems.q: Write a pytest test for a function normalize(x) that should return a vector with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
solution: The tolerance is needed because the mean is computed in floating point and may differ from 0 by rounding error.
problems.a: A test that asserts the mean is 0 (with an absolute tolerance) and the standard deviation is 1.

problems.q: A repository has 1000 commits, and a bug appeared somewhere between commit 1 (good) and commit 1000 (bad). About how many commits does git bisect have to test?
problems.solution: Each test halves the range, so about log₂(1000) ≈ 10 tests.

problems.q: A new 10-class classifier with random weights shows an initial cross-entropy of 2.31 on balanced data. Is that plausible?
problems.solution: Yes: for random weights the predicted distribution is nearly uniform, and the cross-entropy is ln 10 = 2.303. A value like 25 would indicate a bug or bad scaling.

problems.q: A gradient check gives a relative difference of 3 × 10⁻² for one layer and 4 × 10⁻⁹ for the others. What does this indicate and what would you try?
problems.solution: The layer with 3 × 10⁻² has a bug in its analytic gradient (or its finite-difference evaluation hits a kink such as a ReLU at zero). Check its derivation, shapes and transposes; test it in isolation on a tiny input; use a smaller eps or a different random point to rule out kinks.
problems.a: The analytic gradient of that layer is probably wrong; test it in isolation.

problems.q: List three things that can make two runs of the same training script give different results, and one way to control each.
problems.solution: Unseeded random initialization or data shuffling (set seeds for Python, NumPy and the framework); different library versions (pin the environment); non-deterministic GPU kernels (enable deterministic algorithms where available, and accept small differences otherwise). Also data order from parallel loaders.
problems.a: Seeds, library versions and GPU non-determinism; control with fixed seeds, pinned environments and deterministic settings.
